EXHAUSTION OF JUDICIAL REMEDIES: WHEN AN UNCHALLENGED ADMINISTRATIVE DECISION BINDS A LATER WRONGFUL-TERMINATION SUIT (CODE CIV. PROC. §§ 1094.5, 1094.6; UNEMP. INS. CODE § 1960; LAB. CODE § 244; WESTLAKE COMMUNITY HOSP. V. SUPERIOR COURT; JOHNSON V. CITY OF LOMA LINDA; SCHIFANDO V. CITY OF LOS ANGELES; CAMPBELL V. REGENTS; MCDONALD V. ANTELOPE VALLEY COMMUNITY COLLEGE DIST.; MURRAY V. ALASKA AIRLINES; FAHLEN V. SUTTER CENTRAL VALLEY HOSPITALS) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee

SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet concerns the employment of Jordan Lee by City of Riverside as Senior Building Inspector, which ended on or about March 12, 2026, and the administrative decision issued by the City Personnel Board on or about June 4, 2026.

It sets out what California law says about the rule sometimes called exhaustion of judicial remedies, or judicial exhaustion: the principle that once a tribunal acting in a quasi-judicial capacity has made findings about a discharge, those findings are binding in a later civil action unless they are set aside in a mandate proceeding. It also sets out where that rule does not reach — internal grievance procedures a claimant never invoked, proceedings that lack judicial character, unemployment insurance appeals, and claims the Legislature has expressly freed from an exhaustion requirement.

The sheet quotes statutes and opinions and describes what the courts held. It does not evaluate the proceeding the City Personnel Board conducted, state whether any deadline has run for Jordan Lee, or predict how any court would treat the findings in that proceeding.

THE WESTLAKE RULE: A QUASI-JUDICIAL DECISION STANDS UNTIL IT IS SET ASIDE
The rule originates in Westlake Community Hosp. v. Superior Court (1976) 17 Cal.3d 465. A hospital's judicial review committee and board of directors revoked a physician's staff privileges. Without seeking mandamus review of that decision, she sued the hospital and the individual decisionmakers in tort. The Supreme Court held that the quasi-judicial decision retains its force until a court sets it aside, so the plaintiff had to overturn it before pursuing the tort claim. The court gave two reasons: respect for the tribunal's quasi-judicial procedure, which a damages suit would circumvent, and a uniform practice of judicial rather than jury review of quasi-judicial decisions. It also described the other side of the rule — once a court in a mandamus proceeding determines that the decision cannot stand, for either a substantive or a procedural defect, the tort action may go forward.

TWO DIFFERENT DOCTRINES: ADMINISTRATIVE EXHAUSTION AND JUDICIAL EXHAUSTION
California courts use the word "exhaustion" for two distinct requirements. Administrative exhaustion is the requirement that a party initiate and complete a particular administrative proceeding before going to court; the Supreme Court has called it a jurisdictional prerequisite. Judicial exhaustion is different: it can arise whether or not the party had to begin the administrative process at all. Once the party has taken an administrative process to decision, and provided the decision is of a sufficiently judicial character to support collateral estoppel, the party must carry that process to completion, including any available judicial route for reversing adverse findings. Failure to do so leaves the findings with binding, preclusive effect. Johnson v. City of Loma Linda states the same distinction and explains that judicial exhaustion exists to avoid giving binding effect to an agency decision that has become final only because the losing party did not pursue the exclusive judicial remedy for reviewing it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Our exhaustion doctrine comes in two forms: administrative and judicial. Administrative exhaustion refers to the requirement that a party initiate, and complete, a particular administrative proceeding before being permitted to proceed in court."
  — McDonald v. Antelope Valley Community College Dist. (2008) 45 Cal.4th 88, 45 Cal.4th 88, 113 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5608076/mcdonald-v-antelope-valley-community-college-district/)

  — McDonald v. Antelope Valley Community College Dist. (2008) 45 Cal.4th 88, 45 Cal.4th 88, 113 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5608076/mcdonald-v-antelope-valley-community-college-district/)

  — Johnson v. City of Loma Linda (2000) 24 Cal.4th 61, 24 Cal.4th 61, 70 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2589859/johnson-v-city-of-loma-linda/)

JOHNSON V. CITY OF LOMA LINDA: UNCHALLENGED CIVIL SERVICE FINDINGS BIND A LATER FEHA CLAIM
Johnson v. City of Loma Linda (2000) 24 Cal.4th 61 carried the Westlake rule into public employment. An assistant city manager who had been laid off pursued the city's internal remedies: the personnel board found that his termination rested on economic rather than discriminatory reasons, and the city council upheld that finding. He then filed with the state civil rights agency, obtained a right-to-sue letter, and sued under the Fair Employment and Housing Act, joining a petition for administrative mandate that he never brought to hearing. The Supreme Court held that because he had not had the adverse finding set aside through judicial review procedures, the finding was binding on his FEHA claims. The court reproduced Westlake's central sentence and explained the consequence of the contrary rule: refusing to give binding effect to quasi-judicial administrative findings would turn such proceedings into rehearsals for litigation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]

  — Johnson v. City of Loma Linda (2000) 24 Cal.4th 61, 24 Cal.4th 61, 65 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2589859/johnson-v-city-of-loma-linda/)
  "We held that “plaintiff must first succeed in overturning the quasi-judicial action before pursuing her tort claim against defendants.”"
  — Johnson v. City of Loma Linda (2000) 24 Cal.4th 61, 24 Cal.4th 61, 70, quoting Westlake Community Hosp. v. Superior Court (1976) 17 Cal.3d 465, 484 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2589859/johnson-v-city-of-loma-linda/)
  "Refusing to give binding effect to the findings of administrative agencies in quasi-judicial proceedings would, as the City of Glendale observes, undermine the efficacy of such proceedings, rendering them in many cases little more than rehearsals for litigation."
  — Johnson v. City of Loma Linda (2000) 24 Cal.4th 61, 24 Cal.4th 61, 72 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2589859/johnson-v-city-of-loma-linda/)
  "We conclude that when, as here, a public employee pursues administrative civil service remedies, receives an adverse finding, and fails to have the finding set aside through judicial review procedures, the adverse finding is binding on discrimination claims under the FEHA."
  — Johnson v. City of Loma Linda (2000) 24 Cal.4th 61, 24 Cal.4th 61, 76 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2589859/johnson-v-city-of-loma-linda/)

A DISAGREEMENT WITHIN JOHNSON ABOUT WHAT WESTLAKE DECIDED
Johnson was unanimous in result but not in reasoning. Justice Werdegar, joined by Justice Kennard, concurred in the judgment and would have decided the case on ordinary administrative collateral estoppel under People v. Sims (1982) 32 Cal.3d 468 rather than on a "requirement of exhaustion of judicial remedies." The concurrence pointed out that Westlake involved a private hospital, that the Westlake court had not rested on preclusion doctrine, and that Westlake therefore said nothing about the preclusive effect of a public employer's personnel board findings. It then stated in terms that the majority had described Westlake inaccurately. The majority answered that Westlake applies to quasi-judicial proceedings conducted by public as well as private entities, relying on the description of Westlake's "context" in Rojo v. Kliger (1990) 52 Cal.3d 65, 86.

The concurrence says so expressly. Both propositions were confirmed in the fetched text, and a phrase-level search-index query restricted to this opinion's cluster returned one hit for the concurrence's sentence. SCHIFANDO: A PUBLIC EMPLOYEE NEED NOT BEGIN THE EMPLOYER'S INTERNAL PROCESS BEFORE SUING UNDER FEHA
Schifando v. City of Los Angeles (2003) 31 Cal.4th 1074 answered the question Johnson left open. A city employee alleging disability discrimination filed with the state civil rights agency and sued without using the internal remedy the city charter provided. The Supreme Court held that a right-to-sue letter is a sufficient prerequisite to an FEHA action and that municipal employees need not exhaust city charter internal remedies first. The court was explicit that this leaves Johnson intact: an employee who does invoke the internal process and receives an adverse quasi-judicial finding is bound by it unless it is set aside by a timely mandamus petition. In the court's framing, the choice belongs to the employee at the outset, but a choice to use the internal machinery carries the consequence Johnson describes.

CAMPBELL V. REGENTS: WHERE NO STATUTE SUPPLIES ITS OWN PROCESS, THE INTERNAL REMEDY MUST BE USED
Campbell v. Regents of University of California (2005) 35 Cal.4th 311 addressed a university employee who sued for retaliatory termination under Government Code section 12653 and Labor Code section 1102.5 without using the university's internal grievance machinery. The Supreme Court held that the exhaustion rule required her to use the university's administrative remedies before suing. It read its earlier cases — Westlake, Rojo and Moreno — as reflecting respect for internal grievance procedures where the Legislature has not mandated an administrative review process of its own, unlike the FEHA. It also tied the two doctrines together: the exhaustion rule extends to employees seeking judicial review of an employer's administrative findings, and judicial review of the administrative determination remains available through administrative mandamus under Code of Civil Procedure section 1094.5.

THE THRESHOLD: THE PROCEEDING MUST HAVE BEEN JUDICIAL IN CHARACTER
Neither preclusion nor judicial exhaustion attaches to every administrative decision. The Supreme Court has listed the indicia of a proceeding undertaken in a judicial capacity: a hearing before an impartial decisionmaker, testimony under oath or affirmation, the ability to subpoena, call, examine and cross-examine witnesses, to introduce documentary evidence and to make oral and written argument, a record of the proceeding, and a written statement of reasons. In McDonald v. Antelope Valley Community College Dist. (2008) 45 Cal.4th 88 the internal proceeding lacked those characteristics and there had been no evidentiary hearing, so the employee was not required to seek judicial relief to set aside the findings or bear the consequences of their binding effect. The court confined that conclusion to the record before it.

THE PRECLUSION REQUIREMENTS BEHIND THE RULE
Judicial exhaustion is described by the Supreme Court as a corollary of collateral estoppel, and the preclusion requirements do the underlying work. Final decisions of administrative agencies acting in a judicial or quasi-judicial capacity can support issue preclusion. The focus is on whether the party to be bound had an adequate opportunity to litigate the issue in the earlier proceeding, and the ultimate inquiry, as People v. Sims (1982) 32 Cal.3d 468 put it, is whether the traditional requirements and policy reasons for collateral estoppel are satisfied by the particular circumstances. In Murray v. Alaska Airlines, Inc. (2010) 50 Cal.4th 860 those circumstances included a claimant who had received an adverse agency finding on causation, had not used his statutory right to a de novo hearing before an administrative law judge, and had not appealed.

WHAT THE MANDATE COURT REVIEWS: CODE OF CIVIL PROCEDURE SECTION 1094.5
Administrative mandate is the procedure by which a quasi-judicial decision is set aside. Section 1094.5 applies where the writ is sought to inquire into the validity of a final administrative order or decision made in a proceeding in which a hearing was required by law, evidence was required to be taken, and fact-finding discretion was vested in the tribunal. The statute directs that the case be heard by the court sitting without a jury. Its inquiry extends to whether the agency proceeded without or in excess of jurisdiction, whether there was a fair trial, and whether there was a prejudicial abuse of discretion; abuse of discretion is established if the agency did not proceed in the manner required by law, if the decision is not supported by the findings, or if the findings are not supported by the evidence. Where the findings are challenged, the court applies its independent judgment on the evidence in cases where it is authorized by law to do so, and otherwise asks whether substantial evidence in the light of the whole record supports the findings.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]

  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1094.5(b), Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1094.5(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1094.5.)

One category of administrative finding is removed from this machinery by statute. A STATUTE CAN DISPLACE THE OVERTURN-FIRST REQUIREMENT: FAHLEN

WHERE THE RULE HAS BEEN HELD NOT TO REACH
Collected from the authorities quoted above, the boundaries the California Supreme Court has drawn are these.

1. An internal remedy never invoked. Schifando holds that a municipal employee need not use a city charter internal remedy before filing an FEHA complaint with the state civil rights agency; McDonald repeats that initiation and completion of such internal proceedings is not a condition precedent to a FEHA claim.

2. A proceeding without judicial character. McDonald holds that where there was no evidentiary hearing and the proceeding lacked testimony under oath, the opportunity to call witnesses and introduce evidence, and a formal record, the employee was not required to seek judicial relief to set aside the findings.

3. Unemployment insurance findings. Unemployment Insurance Code section 1960 makes appeals board findings neither binding nor admissible in a separate action between an employee and a present or prior employer.

4. A statutory right the Legislature did not condition on mandamus. Fahlen holds that Health and Safety Code section 1278.5 does not require a whistleblower to overturn the hospital's decision first.

5. Claims under the Labor Code, to an extent that remains unsettled. Labor Code section 244(a) removes an exhaustion requirement for civil actions under that code unless the section sued upon expressly requires exhaustion; how far that displaces Campbell has divided the lower courts and the Supreme Court has not spoken.

Each of these is stated as the cited authority states it. None of them is a statement about the proceeding before the City Personnel Board or about any claim Jordan Lee may have.

The rule originates in Westlake Community Hosp. v. Superior Court (1976) 17 Cal.3d 465. A hospital's judicial review committee and board of directors revoked a physician's staff privileges. expectedJSON.body: California courts use the word "exhaustion" for two distinct requirements. Administrative exhaustion is the requirement that a party initiate and complete a particular administrative proceeding before going to court; the Supreme Court has called it a jurisdictional prerequisite. Judicial exhaustion is different: it can arise whether or not the party had to begin the administrative process at all. Once the party has taken an administrative process to decision, and provided the decision is of a sufficiently judicial character to support collateral estoppel, the party must carry that process to completion, including any available judicial route for reversing adverse findings. Failure to do so leaves the findings with binding, preclusive effect. Johnson v. City of Loma Linda states the same distinction and explains that judicial exhaustion exists to avoid giving binding effect to an agency decision that has become final only because the losing party did not pursue the exclusive judicial remedy for reviewing it.

expectedJSON.body: Judicial exhaustion is described by the Supreme Court as a corollary of collateral estoppel, and the preclusion requirements do the underlying work. Final decisions of administrative agencies acting in a judicial or quasi-judicial capacity can support issue preclusion. The focus is on whether the party to be bound had an adequate opportunity to litigate the issue in the earlier proceeding, and the ultimate inquiry, as People v. Sims (1982) 32 Cal.3d 468 put it, is whether the traditional requirements and policy reasons for collateral estoppel are satisfied by the particular circumstances. In Murray v. Alaska Airlines, Inc. (2010) 50 Cal.4th 860 those circumstances included a claimant who had received an adverse agency finding on causation, had not used his statutory right to a de novo hearing before an administrative law judge, and had not appealed.

expectedJSON.body: Administrative mandate is the procedure by which a quasi-judicial decision is set aside. Section 1094.5 applies where the writ is sought to inquire into the validity of a final administrative order or decision made in a proceeding in which a hearing was required by law, evidence was required to be taken, and fact-finding discretion was vested in the tribunal. The statute directs that the case be heard by the court sitting without a jury. Its inquiry extends to whether the agency proceeded without or in excess of jurisdiction, whether there was a fair trial, and whether there was a prejudicial abuse of discretion; abuse of discretion is established if the agency did not proceed in the manner required by law, if the decision is not supported by the findings, or if the findings are not supported by the evidence. Where the findings are challenged, the court applies its independent judgment on the evidence in cases where it is authorized by law to do so, and otherwise asks whether substantial evidence in the light of the whole record supports the findings.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1094.5(b)
citations.quote: The inquiry in such a case shall extend to the questions whether the respondent has proceeded without, or in excess of, jurisdiction; whether there was a fair trial; and whether there was any prejudicial abuse of discretion. Abuse of discretion is established if the respondent has not proceeded in the manner required by law, the order or decision is not supported by the findings, or the findings are not supported by the evidence.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1094.5(c)
citations.quote: Where it is claimed that the findings are not supported by the evidence, in cases in which the court is authorized by law to exercise its independent judgment on the evidence, abuse of discretion is established if the court determines that the findings are not supported by the weight of the evidence. In all other cases, abuse of discretion is established if the court determines that the findings are not supported by substantial evidence in the light of the whole record.

expectedJSON.body: One category of administrative finding is removed from this machinery by statute. Unemployment Insurance Code section 1960 provides that findings, judgments, conclusions and final orders made in proceedings before the California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board are neither conclusive nor binding in a separate or subsequent action between an individual and a present or prior employer, and may not be used as evidence in such an action, regardless of whether the earlier action involved the same or related parties or the same facts. A decision that a claimant was or was not discharged for misconduct therefore does not carry the preclusive consequences that Westlake, Johnson and Murray attach to other quasi-judicial findings, and the mandate route those cases describe is not the mechanism by which such a finding is deprived of effect.

expectedJSON.body: Fahlen v. Sutter Central Valley Hospitals (2014) 58 Cal.4th 655 shows that the Westlake requirement yields where the Legislature has provided otherwise. Collected from the authorities quoted above, the boundaries the California Supreme Court has drawn are these.

1. An internal remedy never invoked. Schifando holds that a municipal employee need not use a city charter internal remedy before filing an FEHA complaint with the state civil rights agency; McDonald repeats that initiation and completion of such internal proceedings is not a condition precedent to a FEHA claim.

2. A proceeding without judicial character. McDonald holds that where there was no evidentiary hearing and the proceeding lacked testimony under oath, the opportunity to call witnesses and introduce evidence, and a formal record, the employee was not required to seek judicial relief to set aside the findings.

3. Unemployment insurance findings. Unemployment Insurance Code section 1960 makes appeals board findings neither binding nor admissible in a separate action between an employee and a present or prior employer.

4. A statutory right the Legislature did not condition on mandamus. Fahlen holds that Health and Safety Code section 1278.5 does not require a whistleblower to overturn the hospital's decision first.

5. Claims under the Labor Code, to an extent that remains unsettled. Labor Code section 244(a) removes an exhaustion requirement for civil actions under that code unless the section sued upon expressly requires exhaustion; how far that displaces Campbell has divided the lower courts and the Supreme Court has not spoken.

Each of these is stated as the cited authority states it. None of them is a statement about the proceeding before the City Personnel Board or about any claim Jordan Lee may have.
